blocks.text: Picture three different companies, each running their own MCP servers, deciding to let each others tools talk to one another. That is federation. No single company owns the whole system.
Federated MCP systems let organizations share capabilities across boundaries without handing control to one central authority. Each org keeps its own server, its own rules, and its own data.
The tradeoff is complexity. Trust has to be negotiated, identity has to cross boundaries safely, and when something breaks, the bug might live in a system your team has never even seen.
What Federated MCP Actually Means

blocks.alt: Several organizations connect their own MCP systems into one federation

blocks.text: A federated MCP system is a group of independently operated MCP servers that agree to work together. Each server belongs to a different organization, but together they behave like one larger network.
Think of it like airlines that codeshare flights. Each airline still owns its own planes and staff, but a passenger can book one trip that spans multiple carriers.

items: Each organization runs and controls its own MCP server
Servers agree on shared protocols for discovery and calls
No single company can shut down the whole federation
Membership can grow or shrink without rebuilding the system

blocks.text: This is different from a plugin marketplace, where one company still approves every listing. In a federation, member organizations approve each other directly.
Why Not Just Build One Central Server
A single central MCP server sounds simpler, but it means one company controls everything. Partners would need to trust that one operator completely.
Federation spreads that control out. Each org keeps ownership of its own data, its own uptime, and its own security posture.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: In real partnerships, no company wants to give a competitor or vendor full control over its data pipeline. Federation lets everyone keep their own house while still sharing a hallway.

blocks.text: This shows up often in healthcare networks, financial consortiums, and research alliances, where each member has strict rules about who can touch their systems.

items: Hospitals sharing appointment availability across networks
Banks sharing fraud signals without sharing account data
Universities sharing research tool access across campuses

blocks.text: The Core Building Blocks of a Federation

blocks.alt: Trust agreements, identity, and discovery together form a federation

blocks.text: Most federated MCP setups share a few common pieces, even if the exact implementation differs between vendors.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","Purpose"],"rows":[["Federation gateway","Routes requests between member servers"],["Trust registry","Records which organizations are approved members"],["Identity broker","Issues tokens that are recognized across org boundaries"],["Capability catalog","Lists which tools each member exposes to others"],["Audit log","Each org keeps its own record of cross org calls"]]}

blocks.text: None of these pieces belong to just one company. Each member typically runs its own copy of the gateway software, configured with its own trust rules.
Trust Agreements Between Organizations

blocks.alt: Organization A and organization B sign a trust agreement before calls flow

blocks.text: Before any server talks to another, the organizations behind them sign a trust agreement. This is part legal contract and part technical configuration.
The technical side usually lives in a config file that both sides load into their gateway.
Notice the small scope list and the short token lifetime. Good trust agreements grant the least access needed and expire quickly.
The reviewCycleDays field matters more than people expect. Without a scheduled review, old trust agreements quietly accumulate access nobody remembers granting.
Identity That Crosses Organizational Boundaries
Inside one company, identity is easy. Everyone trusts the same login system. Across companies, that assumption breaks down.
Federated MCP systems solve this with signed tokens that carry proof of who issued them and what they are allowed to do.
The remote server does not need to know Jane personally. It only needs to trust the issuer and check the scopes on the token.

items: iss tells the remote server who issued the token
aud tells the remote server the token was meant for them specifically
scopes tells the remote server exactly what is allowed
exp keeps the window of trust short

blocks.text: How a Cross Organization Call Flows

blocks.alt: A call from one organization flows across the boundary into another organization

blocks.text: When a user asks their assistant to do something that touches a partner org, several hops happen behind the scenes.

items: The home gateway checks if the request needs a remote capability
It looks up the trust agreement for that partner
The identity broker issues a short lived cross org token
The remote gateway validates the token against the trust registry
The remote server executes the call and logs it locally
Both sides record the transaction in their own audit logs

blocks.text: Every one of those hops adds latency and a place where things can go wrong. A federation with three or four partners in one call chain needs to plan for that.
Discovering What Partners Can Do
Before any call can happen, a server needs to know what its partners actually offer. That is the job of a capability catalog.
Each member publishes a small manifest describing its tools, without exposing internal implementation details.
Catalogs should stay small and honest. Listing a capability that is not actually reliable just creates confusion for every partner relying on it.
Governance Without a Central Authority

blocks.alt: No single central authority governs a federation, each member governs its own part

blocks.text: Federations still need rules, even without one company in charge. Usually a small governance group made of member representatives handles this.
Decisions like adding a new member, removing a bad actor, or changing shared protocol versions get voted on rather than dictated.

blocks.title: Common pattern
blocks.content: Many federations start with two or three founding members who write the first trust rules, then open membership to new partners who agree to the same terms.

items: Approving new members joining the federation
Removing a member that violates the trust agreement
Updating shared protocol versions everyone must support
Resolving disputes when two members disagree on scope

blocks.text: Security Considerations at the Boundary
The organizational boundary is the riskiest part of the whole system. A weak trust check there can expose one org to a compromised partner.

items: Always verify token signatures against the issuers published keys
Keep cross org token lifetimes short
Scope tokens tightly instead of granting broad access
Check a revocation list before honoring any token
Rotate signing keys on a schedule both sides agree to

blocks.text: A single missed check at the boundary can undo all the careful design inside each individual server, so this deserves extra review time.
Data Residency and Privacy Across Members
Different organizations often operate under different privacy laws or internal policies. Federation has to respect that instead of assuming one common rulebook.
A trust agreement usually spells out what data can leave an org, what must stay local, and how long logs are retained.

items: What fields can be shared in a response versus kept local
How long each side is allowed to retain shared data
Which legal jurisdiction governs a dispute
What happens to shared data if the trust agreement ends

blocks.text: Debugging a Problem That Spans Multiple Owners
This is the hard part. When a federated call fails, the bug could be in your gateway, the partner server, the identity broker, or the network between them.
No single team has full visibility, and no single team has permission to see everyone elses logs.

items: Start by confirming which side rejected or failed the call
Check token validity and scopes before assuming a code bug
Ask the partner team for their audit log entry with the matching request id
Compare timestamps carefully, since clock drift between orgs is common
Escalate through the governance contact if the partner team is unresponsive

blocks.content: {"headers":["Symptom","Likely owner to check first"],"rows":[["Token rejected immediately","Identity broker or trust registry"],["Call succeeds but wrong data returned","Remote org server logic"],["Call times out with no response","Network path or remote gateway"],["Works for one partner, fails for another","That specific trust agreement config"]]}

blocks.text: Correlation Ids Make Cross Org Debugging Possible

blocks.alt: A correlation id follows a request as it crosses organizational boundaries

blocks.text: The single most useful habit in a federation is attaching one shared request id to every hop of a call.
Without it, matching a failure on one side to a log entry on the other side becomes guesswork.
Agree on the request id format before launch, not after the first incident. Retrofitting tracing into a live federation is much harder than starting with it.
Versioning When Nobody Controls the Release Schedule
In a normal system, one team can upgrade everything together. In a federation, each org ships on its own schedule.
This means the protocol between members has to tolerate old and new versions running side by side for a while.

blocks.title: Practical tip
blocks.content: Always include a version field in the trust config and capability catalog. Reject unknown fields gracefully instead of crashing, so a partners upgrade does not break your server.

blocks.text: Treat every partner interface as something that will change without your permission or your calendar. Defensive parsing saves a lot of late night pages.
When Federation Is the Wrong Tool

blocks.alt: A small team within one organization points away from federation

blocks.text: Federation adds real overhead. If you only have one team and one server, none of this trust and identity machinery is worth building.
It earns its keep when multiple independent organizations genuinely need to share capabilities while keeping their own operational control.
If you find yourself building trust agreements between two teams inside the same company, that is usually a sign you need better internal permissions, not a federation.
Worked Example
Two hospital networks, org-alpha and org-beta, want their scheduling assistants to check each others open appointment slots without sharing patient records.
They sign a trust agreement that only allows the scope appointments.read, with a five minute token lifetime.

items: A patient at org-alpha asks the assistant for the next open slot at either hospital
The home gateway sees the request needs org-beta data and checks the trust registry
The identity broker issues a scoped token good for five minutes
Org-betas gateway validates the token and scope, then calls its own scheduling server
Org-beta returns only open slot times, no patient details
Both sides log the request id, so a support ticket later can be traced on both ends

blocks.text: When a patient later reports a missing slot, the support teams pull up the shared request id and find the exact hop where the call failed, instead of guessing.
Common Mistakes

items: Granting broad scopes because it is easier than defining narrow ones
Skipping revocation checks and trusting a token until it naturally expires
Not agreeing on a shared request id format before going live
Assuming clocks are synced across organizations without checking
Treating the trust agreement as a one time setup instead of reviewing it regularly
Building debugging tools that only work with your own logs, not your partners

blocks.text: Practice
Sketch a trust agreement for two fictional companies that want to share a customer support MCP tool.

items: Decide what scopes each side actually needs, and make them as narrow as possible
Write a short cross org token payload with an issuer, audience, and expiry
Draw the request flow for one call that crosses the boundary and back
List three things that could break the call and who would need to be involved to debug each one

blocks.text: If you have access to a sandbox, try building the trust config as a real json file and validating it against the token example above.
Key Takeaway

Federated MCP systems let independent organizations share capabilities without one company owning everything. That freedom comes from trust agreements and cross org identity, not from a central server.
The cost is debugging difficulty. When a call spans multiple owners, correlation ids, clear scopes, and good communication between teams are what actually save you.
